startup.name: Salem Robotics Inc
startup.one_liner: Deploying robots to replace workers in hazardous spaces
startup.description: Software that turns deployed robots into independent workers in hazardous facilities, starting in nuclear. They walk sites, handle instruments, collect measurements and generate auditable compliance records. Two founders from Los Alamos robotics and deterministic manipulation research. Buyers would be nuclear operators and similar regulated industries.

yc_acceptance.basis: Note only because the company is already accepted. A random applicant starts near 1 percent. Domain founders from a national lab, a hard tech wedge aligned with YC interest in robotics, energy and defense, and a regulated customer pull would lift this far above the base.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because nuclear sales cycles are long, the buyers are few and hard to reach, and a two person team would depend on robots it does not build. A reviewer might also ask whether a software claim hides a hardware services business that cannot reach revenue within a batch.

ladder.why_it_fails: The seed stalls if there is no paid pilot at a nuclear site, because investors cannot judge the sales cycle and security approvals take many months. Two founders cannot build manipulation software, integrate robots and navigate licensing together. Analogs such as Orangewood Labs raised a small round and moved slowly, and hardware companies often take years to reach a priced seed.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A fails if pilots do not convert to recurring contracts. Nuclear operators move slowly and may prefer proven vendors such as Boston Dynamics integrators. Without a repeatable deployment kit, each site is a custom project, which investors treat as services revenue. Atomic Alchemy and Bear Flag show niche hard tech can be bought, but neither reached a large independent round.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B needs deployments across several industries and robots that work unattended, with safety certification. If every site needs custom tuning or a human tele operator, margins look like services. Robotics hardware dependence also exposes the company to supplier changes. Investors would also compare the company with the closest analogs in the data, most of which stalled at this step without clear revenue or a durable advantage over better funded rivals.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Failure paths are slow sales to few buyers, hardware dependence and a thin runway for a two person team. If pilots stay unpaid or regulators demand extensive qualification, the company runs out of money before any contract renews. Many hard tech analogs end as small acquisitions by larger industrial or defense firms.

killers.risk: Nuclear and regulated buyers take years to buy and the team runs out of runway
killers.evidence: Spot has been used at Fukushima and Dounreay in projects that took long and came from operators with large budgets, not startups.
killers.mitigation: Start with a lower security site such as decommissioning or a national lab pilot and get one paid contract.

killers.risk: Incumbent robot makers and integrators win the same work
killers.evidence: Boston Dynamics already markets Spot for radiation mapping at several sites and integrators add arms and sensors.
killers.mitigation: Own the manipulation and audit record software and stay robot agnostic.

killers.risk: Autonomous manipulation is not reliable enough to replace workers
killers.evidence: Handling instruments and overcoming obstacles unattended remains a research problem, and failures in a hazardous site are costly.
killers.mitigation: Ship supervised autonomy with a remote operator and measure intervention rate.

killers.risk: Two person team spread across hardware, software and compliance
killers.evidence: The company expects to expand to other hazardous industries before proving one. and this pattern is visible in the cited analogs.
killers.mitigation: Hire a robotics engineer and a safety lead early and keep one wedge.

competition_now.traction: Independent coverage by World Nuclear News

competition_now.what: Manual surveys and inspections, the status quo
competition_now.traction: Mandated by regulation, which is the spend to replace

technical_complexity.rationale: Reliable manipulation of instruments, navigation of obstacles and creation of auditable records in radiation environments needs hardened robots and strong software. A two person team can demo a robot task but cannot certify it in three months, so the hard parts are a risk now and a moat only if solved.

takeover_risk.rationale: Robot makers and integrators can add arms and software but nuclear qualification and the audit record take time. The risk is moderate because buyers are few and slow, which also slows copying.

evidence.claim: Operators already use Spot for radiation surveys at Fukushima Daiichi, Dounreay and Chernobyl, so the use case is real and funded.
Manual surveys are mandatory and a robot reduces worker dose, as Boston Dynamics case studies describe.

roadmap.goal: A paid pilot at one hazardous site with a measured intervention rate.
actions: Sign a paid pilot at a national lab or decommissioning site.
Measure survey hours replaced and the auditable record quality.
roadmap.proof: One paid pilot and a documented drop in manual survey hours.

roadmap.goal: Repeatable deployment kit across two industries.
actions: Package the software for two robot platforms.
Win a second hazardous industry customer.
roadmap.proof: Three paying sites and recurring annual contracts.

brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Salem Robotics Inc" --era 2022+ : kind name_plus_descriptor, alive 93.7 percent in cohort n=557
weaknesses: Inc suffix and generic descriptor are forgettable
Salem evokes witch trials more than hazard work
brand.rationale: A descriptor name that tells buyers the category but has no distinct identity. Cohort data show name plus descriptor companies survive at about the same rate as others, and nuclear buyers choose on trust and credentials rather than names.

narrative.headline: A credible lab pedigree in a real but slow market, likely to raise a seed and then depend on converting pilots.
narrative.general_summary: Salem Robotics aims to put robots to work in hazardous sites, starting in nuclear. Existing robot deployments at Fukushima and Dounreay show demand, and mandatory surveys give a clear thing to replace. The founders have the right background, but it is only two people and the work involves hardware, manipulation and regulatory qualification. A seed above the YC check is likely given the pull for energy, defense and robotics. Series A depends on paid pilots turning into recurring contracts. About 40 percent of forecast paths end in a stall or shutdown.

assumptions: Blind forecast as of 2026-07-06 using only the batch listing.
Industrials cohorts are tiny (n=11 to 12) so base rates are anecdotes; B2B was used as a cross check.
The step seed means a round above about $500K within roughly 12 months of the batch start.
